newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's LTCB working on boosting its profitability.
newsitem.headline: Japan's LTCB working on boosting its profitability.

text.p: The Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan (LTCB) is aggressively trying to improve the quality of its assets and distinguish itself from its numerous rivals amid fierce competition in the Japanese market, company officials say.

"Japanese banks currently have similar faces," Kazuhiko Oiwa, director and general manager at LTCB's corporate planning division, told Reuters in a recent interview. "We want to make it clear what our strategy is as a wholesale bank."

Oiwa said his bank would maintain its status as a wholesale lender and at the same time strengthen its investment banking business. LTCB also plans to establish a trust banking unit in the latter half of the current business year ending March 1997.
LTCB, ranked as the world's 20th biggest bank in terms of assets, provides long-term funds to corporations and currently has about 8,000 corporate customers.

It raises funds mainly through debentures rather than by taking deposits from individuals. Thus it has only a small network of domestic branches -- less than one-tenth of the more than 300 branches which other big commercial banks can boast.
Analysts say LTCB has been aggressive in restructuring its operations and boosting its competitiveness in special fields such as derivatives and consulting.
The bank said earlier this year that under its restructuring plan, it would cut its assets by 1.3 trillion yen ($11.7 billion) in the next two years.

It plans to achieve this by cutting less profitable loan assets by one trillion yen ($9.0 billion) by March 31, 1997 and selling shareholdings worth 300 billion yen ($2.70 billion) by March 31, 1998. As of the end of March, its assets totalled 29.52 trillion yen ($265 billion).

Earlier this year, it sold its Belgian unit LTCB (Europe) to Banque Paribas Belgique, closed its representative offices in Milan and Melbourne, and announced it would sell its U.S. securities business unit to Britain's National Westminster Bank Plc.
"We are meeting the challenge of cutting our assets, which have swollen too much," Oiwa said.

In 1995/96 ended March 31, it posted a parent current loss of 110.48 billion yen ($995 million) as it disposed of problem loans of 650 billion yen ($5.85 billion), including those to failed housing loan firms. In 1996/97, it expects parent current profit of 20 billion yen ($180 million) while disposing of problem loans of more than 100 billion yen ($900 million).
Analysts said it may be another few years before LTCB can reduce problem loans to manageable levels from the 1.2 trillion yen ($10.8 billion) of such loans it had as of end-March.

Oiwa said the bank's restructuring plan is contributing to its earnings for the current year to some extent. It is aiming to improve profits by 30 billion yen ($270 million) each year through the restructuring programme.

An analyst at a foreign brokerage said: "Considering its strength in derivatives and strong business ties with big- and medium-sized corporations, I expect it will go along as a bank with special features."
However, he said there was some doubt about opportunities for growth in light of mounting competition in domestic markets amid the ongoing financial deregulation.

Asked about the possibility of a merger with another bank in the future, Oiwa did not deny such a possibility but said: "We are not considering merging with another bank now and will not think about that for the time being... We are busy becoming slimmer and more attractive now." ($1=111 yen)
